Based on your six documents, three HRIS apps clearly meet your free/under-$5/month and desktop-usable criteria, plus one platform worth learning specifically for its partner program (the actual path to contracts/partnerships), even though it doesn't meet the low-cost bar itself.

**Zoho People** is the strongest pick. Its Free plan covers up to 5 users, and if you outgrow that, Essential HR runs $1.50-$3/user/month - both under your $5 ceiling (Workforce and Talent tiers hit exactly $5, so stay on Essential HR to stay clear of that line). It's a full browser-based HRIS usable on any desktop or laptop, backed by a large ecosystem (50,000+ businesses, per its own pricing page) and a visible Partners section in its navigation - meaning Zoho already has a structure for consultants and implementers to formalize relationships with the platform. For someone with your HR Generalist/Manager background, Zoho People is common enough among small businesses that fluency in it is a credible line item when pitching HR advisory or HRIS-setup services.

**TalentHR** is genuinely free forever for up to 10 users (not a disguised trial), with paid tiers at $2 and $4/user/month if you need performance reviews or time tracking - both under $5. It's desktop/web-based, and because HiBob's own competitor review flagged its only real con as scaling limits past very small teams, it's ideal as a low-stakes sandbox to build hands-on configuration skills (onboarding workflows, time-off policies, reporting) that translate directly into "I can set this up for your business" conversations with prospective clients.

**HR.my** is free for unlimited users indefinitely, with payroll, leave, attendance, and document workflow - useful mainly as a zero-cost option to point extremely budget-conscious prospects toward, though it lacks a formal support contract, which matters if you're recommending it to a client.

Worth naming what to skip: BambooHR and Gusto are frequently cited as "best for small business," but per both the Paychex and TalentHR documents, BambooHR has no free plan (trial only, quote-based pricing) and Gusto starts at $40/month plus $6/user - both fail your cost constraint despite their popularity.

The BD angle you specifically asked about - turning platform knowledge into contracts or partnerships - points most directly at **Rippling's Partner Ecosystem** (rippling.com/partners). Rippling explicitly runs Technology, Service, Accountant, Broker, and VC partner tracks with over 1,500 partners already enrolled and 20,000+ client companies to be introduced to. Service and Accountant partners get matched with clients needing implementation, training, and ongoing HR support - which is a direct pipeline to paid engagements, not just software literacy. Rippling itself isn't free (other research cites pricing starting around $8+/user/month, above your ceiling as an end customer), but exploring its Help Center, API documentation, and App Shop to understand the platform costs nothing, and partner enrollment is a separate track from paying for a seat. Given your HR background, this is the one platform where the "partnership" outcome you asked about is a built-in program rather than an inferred benefit.

**Practical sequencing:** build core configuration fluency in Zoho People and TalentHR first (both cheap, both desktop-based, both common among small-business prospects), then use that hands-on credibility to explore whether Rippling's Service or Accountant partner track fits your consulting goals.

**The four platforms worth learning first, regardless of what kind of HR job you're chasing:**

Workday is the single most valuable platform to know. It holds roughly 33.8% of the core HR software market and about 32% of enterprise ATS share, with over 33,500 companies running it (74% of them in the US). Indeed and ZipRecruiter listings for HR Coordinator, HRIS Analyst, and HR Generalist roles name Workday more often than any other single system - it shows up whether the req is entry-level or senior, and it appears independently in three of your uploaded documents (Paylocity's comparison, the Peoplebox "Top 30" roundup, and the Workable vs. Workday guide) as the default enterprise standard.

ADP Workforce Now is next, mainly because ADP is the largest payroll provider in the world, so "ADP experience" appears constantly in postings even for companies that don't use ADP as their full HRIS - payroll and compliance fluency transfers. UKG Pro/Ready and SAP SuccessFactors round out the top four; search results and your Paylocity document both show these three named alongside Workday as the systems employers list together ("familiarity with ADP, Workday, or Dayforce" is close to boilerplate phrasing in HR job ads now).

**Named by name in specific postings:** Paycom and Ceridian Dayforce show up often enough as explicit line items - some HRIS Lead postings specifically ask for "1-2 years of hands-on Paycom experience" - that they're worth flagging even though their overall market share is smaller than the big four.

**If you're targeting small-business HR roles instead of enterprise:** BambooHR is the SMB default (both your Peoplebox doc and Paylocity's own comparison call it out as the go-to for lean HR teams), and Paylocity, Gusto, Rippling, and Zoho People all show up repeatedly as the systems small and midsize employers actually run day to day. Zoho People is notably the cheapest named option in your Paylocity document at $1.25/employee/month, which matters if you're advising or supporting cost-conscious employers rather than just working inside a large system.

**If you're pursuing recruiting/talent acquisition roles specifically, not general HR:** the ATS layer matters more than the HRIS layer. Workday Recruiting again leads (~32%), followed by Greenhouse (~18%), Lever (~12%), and iCIMS (~10%). Workable is the volume leader in the SMB/mid-market ATS space with over 20,000 customers, per your uploaded comparison - useful if you're eyeing recruiting-coordinator roles at smaller companies rather than enterprise TA jobs.

One flag on that Workable-vs-Workday document: it's a vendor comparison page from a company called MokaHR, and it's structured to steer the reader toward MokaHR at every turn (inserted "you might also consider MokaHR" language, unverifiable stats like "87% match accuracy" and customer claims about Tesla/Nestle, plus fake-looking academic citations). I pulled the factual Workable/Workday split from it but didn't treat MokaHR's own claims as verified - it's marketing copy, not a neutral source, and MokaHR doesn't otherwise show up as a real market player in the job-posting or market-share data I found.

**Bottom line for staying competitive as a candidate with your HR background:** Workday first, ADP and UKG close behind, SAP SuccessFactors if you're eyeing global/multinational employers, and BambooHR or Paylocity if you're aiming at the small-business market instead. Paycom and Ceridian Dayforce are worth a working knowledge of even if you don't get hands-on practice, since they appear by name often enough in postings that recognizing them signals fluency.
